description: The SELECT column list is missing commas between column names, causing a syntax error. Fix the query so it correctly retrieves id, username, and email from the users table.
broken_query: SELECT id username email FROM users;
gold_query: SELECT id, username, email FROM users;
hints: Check the column list in the SELECT statement.
SQL requires a comma separating each selected column.

description: The query joins users and orders but references 'id' without a table prefix. SQLite raises 'ambiguous column name: id' because both tables have an id column. Fix the query by qualifying the column with its table name so it returns each user's username alongside their order id.
broken_query: SELECT username, id FROM users JOIN orders ON users.id = orders.user_id;
gold_query: SELECT users.username, orders.id FROM users JOIN orders ON users.id = orders.user_id;
hints: When two tables share a column name, SQLite cannot tell which one you mean.
Prefix the ambiguous column with its table name, e.g. orders.id.
Both tables have an 'id' column — be explicit about which one you want.

description: The query uses INNER JOIN which excludes users with no orders. Some users in the system have never placed an order — they must still appear in the results (with NULL for the order id). Fix the join type to include ALL users.
broken_query: SELECT users.username, orders.id FROM users INNER JOIN orders ON users.id = orders.user_id;
gold_query: SELECT users.username, orders.id FROM users LEFT JOIN orders ON users.id = orders.user_id;
hints: What happens if a user has never placed an order?
Consider using an outer join to include all left-hand records regardless of a match.
INNER JOIN only returns rows where a match exists in both tables.

description: The query uses COUNT(*) but the task requires summing the total_amount spent per user, not counting the number of orders. Fix the aggregation function.
broken_query: SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) as total_spent FROM orders GROUP BY user_id;
gold_query: SELECT user_id, SUM(total_amount) as total_spent FROM orders GROUP BY user_id;
hints: Are you counting rows or summing a numeric value?
Replace COUNT(*) with an aggregation that adds up amounts.
The column you need to aggregate is total_amount.

description: The correlated subquery in the SELECT clause executes once per product row (N+1 problem), which is extremely slow at scale. Rewrite the query to use a single JOIN + GROUP BY instead. Also note: products with no order items must show 0 (not NULL) for total_sold.
broken_query: SELECT id, name, (SELECT SUM(quantity) FROM order_items WHERE product_id = products.id) AS total_sold FROM products;
gold_query: SELECT products.id, products.name, COALESCE(SUM(order_items.quantity), 0) AS total_sold FROM products LEFT JOIN order_items ON products.id = order_items.product_id GROUP BY products.id, products.name;
hints: Avoid subqueries in the SELECT clause for large tables — they cause N+1 scans.
Join the tables and use GROUP BY to aggregate in a single pass.
Use COALESCE to convert NULL to 0 for products with no orders.
The correct approach: LEFT JOIN order_items ON products.id = order_items.product_id
